intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, gives you something to remember and warns you where practice slips. Work the section exercises in pencil, answer the recall questions before you check, and use the margins for the rules you must verify locally.

sections.title: What SRHR Means
sections.big_idea: SRHR is health, dignity and rights across the whole life course, for everyone. **A service that covers only reproduction has left out the S and the second R.**
in_plain_words: WHO defines sexual health as physical, emotional, mental and social well-being in relation to sexuality, including the possibility of pleasurable and safe experiences free of coercion. The four letters are Sexual, Reproductive, Health and Rights. Programmes usually deliver the R and the H and omit the S and the second R, which gives maternal and child health under a wider name.

Services are built around the married woman of reproductive age, so childhood, adolescence and later life go underserved. The cause is rarely a law: the care is simply not commissioned, staffed or measured. Inclusion covers unmarried people, LGBTQ+ people, persons with disabilities, older people and men. Language is the first thing a patient assesses, so choose it with care.

diagram.caption: SRHR runs the whole life course, yet services cluster in the third stage

key_terms.meaning: Physical, emotional, mental and social well-being in relation to sexuality.
Sexual and reproductive health and rights: four letters, all of which a service should cover.
Childhood to later life; SRHR needs change at each stage.
The target on decision-making over one's own body; indicator 5.6.1 measures autonomy.
Neutral words, open questions and correct anatomical terms.

worked_example.title: Swap the words
worked_example.setup: A counsellor's script contains four phrases from the deck's list of language to avoid. Replace each.
steps: 'Promiscuous' or 'loose' becomes a description of behaviour, because judgement stops disclosure.
'Your husband' becomes 'your partner', or simply ask, since the first presumes marriage and heterosexuality.
'Clean' for STI-negative becomes 'negative' or 'no infection', since 'clean' makes infection a moral state.
'Failed to use protection' becomes 'was not able to use', which stops locating the problem in the person.
worked_example.answer: Four swaps that keep the patient talking and keep the history accurate.

mistakes: Equating SRHR with maternal and child health. That delivers the R and the H and omits the S and the second R.
Assuming the gap is legal. The deck says very little of what these groups need is prohibited.
Framing a service for the married woman only, so unmarried people, men and older people never see themselves in it.
Dropping WHO's clause on pleasurable and safe experiences, which is the part that lets a service detect coercion.

recall.q: Name the four letters of SRHR.
recall.a: Sexual, Reproductive, Health and Rights.

recall.q: What is the test of whether a service covers all four letters?
recall.a: Whether it serves an unmarried person who is not pregnant and does not want to be.

recall.q: Which two SDG targets does the deck contrast, and how?
recall.a: 3.7 measures service access and 5.6 measures whether the person decides.

recall.q: Name three groups that default assumptions exclude.
recall.a: Any three of unmarried people, LGBTQ+ people, persons with disabilities, older people, men.

recall.q: Why does the deck say language matters?
recall.a: Patients assess it in the first thirty seconds and it determines what they tell you.

sections.title: The Rights Framework
sections.big_idea: SRHR applies existing human rights to sexuality and reproduction. **Cairo 1994 replaced targets with choice**, and bodily autonomy is the core principle.
in_plain_words: No new rights were invented. Life, privacy, equality, freedom from ill-treatment and information are applied to sexuality and reproduction, so claims are enforceable. The ICPD in Cairo in 1994, endorsed by 179 governments, moved the agenda from population targets to individual rights. India dropped method-specific targets in 1996, and Devika Biswas (2016) closed sterilisation camps and set consent standards.

Bodily autonomy means saying yes, saying no and deciding whether and when to have children, free from coercion in either direction. The 2018 Guttmacher–Lancet definition gave a checkable package of seven elements. AAAQ (available, accessible, acceptable, quality) is a conjunction: a clinic that shames patients delivers nothing, because acceptability gates the rest.

left.title: Before ICPD
items: The person is a unit of the target

right.title: After ICPD
items: Success: need met, quality of care

key_terms.meaning: The right to decide freely the number, spacing and timing of children, with the means to do so.
The 1994 Cairo conference, endorsed by 179 governments.
Making decisions about one's own body and future, free from coercion.
Available, accessible, acceptable and quality, from General Comment 14.
The 2018 Commission that defined an essential SRHR package.

worked_example.title: Score a clinic on AAAQ
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a clinic has free, well-stocked contraceptives, but staff judge unmarried clients and the consultation room has no privacy.
steps: Available: services and supplies exist and are stocked, so this passes.
Accessible: refusing to serve unmarried people fails the non-discrimination test.
Acceptable: judgemental staff and no privacy fail dignity and confidentiality.
The four elements are a conjunction, so failing acceptability gates the rest.
worked_example.answer: The clinic fails on accessibility and acceptability, so its stock delivers nothing.

mistakes: Treating SRHR rights as aspirational. They are established human rights applied to a new area.
Reading Cairo as mere rhetoric. It changed the measure of success from acceptors to need met and quality of care.
Missing coercion in the second direction: pressure to bear children is the same violation as pressure to be sterilised.
Scoring AAAQ as a sum. A clinic strong on three and weak on acceptability still fails.

recall.q: How many governments endorsed the Cairo Programme of Action?
In what year did India abolish method-specific targets?
What did Devika Biswas (2016) order?
recall.a: Closure of sterilisation camps and standards for consent and post-operative care.

recall.q: What four things does AAAQ stand for?
recall.a: Availability, accessibility, acceptability and quality.

recall.q: What did the Guttmacher–Lancet Commission add?
recall.a: A checkable essential package, so 'we provide SRHR' could be tested.

sections.title: Bodies & Puberty
sections.big_idea: Accurate, shame-free body knowledge is health care and child protection. **Variation is normal**, and distress usually comes from missing information.
in_plain_words: Correct anatomical words let a child describe what happened and let a person consent or refuse. Puberty usually begins between about 8 and 14, and timing varies widely. The menstrual cycle averages about 28 days, but anything from 21 to 35 is normal. The luteal phase is steady at about 14 days, and the follicular phase is what varies.

That is why 'day 14' is unreliable, and why fertility awareness shows a wide gap between typical and perfect use. Menstrual health needs materials, a private space with water and soap, safe disposal and information before menarche. Restrictions on kitchens and temples have no health basis, and seclusion can kill. Very heavy, painful or absent periods deserve a check-up.

diagram.caption: the follicular phase varies; the luteal phase is the stable part

key_terms.meaning: The transition to reproductive maturity, usually beginning between about 8 and 14.
The first period; irregular cycles are common in the two years after it.
The steady final phase of the cycle, about 14 days.
Menstrual health and hygiene: materials, privacy, water, disposal and information.
The days around ovulation when pregnancy is most likely.

worked_example.title: Why day 14 fails
worked_example.setup: Use the luteal phase of about 14 days to place ovulation in three cycles of different length.
steps: 28-day cycle: ovulation = 28 − 14 = 14, so day 14.
35-day cycle: ovulation = 35 − 14 = 21, so day 21.
21-day cycle: ovulation = 21 − 14 = 7, so day 7.
All three cycles are within the normal range of 21 to 35 days.
worked_example.answer: Ovulation falls on day 14, 21 or 7, so a fixed 'day 14' rule is unreliable.

mistakes: Using calendar prediction in the first two years after menarche or near menopause, when it is least reliable.
Treating menstrual restrictions as health requirements. The deck finds no health basis for any of them.
Arguing with the belief when the practical fix is toilets, materials and pain relief.
Normalising pain that stops school or work. Endometriosis is typically diagnosed years late.

recall.q: Within what age range does puberty usually begin?
recall.a: Roughly 8 to 14.

recall.q: What range of cycle length is normal?
recall.a: Roughly 21 to 35 days.

recall.q: Which phase of the cycle is stable?
recall.a: The luteal phase, about 14 days.

recall.q: Why is information before menarche often mistimed?
recall.a: Sessions are scheduled for classes where many girls have already started.

recall.q: Which symptom should never be normalised?
recall.a: Bleeding after sex.

sections.title: Contraception & Family Planning
sections.big_idea: Family planning prevents unintended pregnancy, and only **informed, voluntary choice** makes it rights-based. Counsel from typical-use figures.
in_plain_words: Methods fall into six families: barrier, short-acting hormonal, long-acting reversible (LARC), permanent, emergency and fertility awareness. Only condoms protect against STIs, so ask both questions at every consultation. Perfect use describes a laboratory, and typical use is what matters: implant and IUD stay above 99%, the pill drops to about 93% and the male condom to about 87%.

Good counselling presents the full range, gives honest side-effect information, asks about STI risk separately, says that switching and stopping are allowed, and guarantees removal on request. India's mix is skewed: female sterilisation about 38% against male about 0.3%. NFHS-6 unmet need is 8.5%, measured only among married women.

diagram.caption: emergency pill and fertility awareness complete the six families

key_terms.meaning: Long-acting reversible contraception: IUD and implant, years of protection.
Effectiveness as the method is used in real life; the number for counselling.
Preventing both pregnancy and STIs, which only condoms do.
Share who want to avoid pregnancy but use no method.
A backup pill that works mainly by delaying or preventing ovulation.

worked_example.title: Perfect use against typical use
worked_example.setup: Using the deck's figures for the pill (perfect use over 99%, typical about 93%) and the male condom (about 98% and about 87%), count pregnancies per 100 users in a year.
steps: Pill under typical use: 100 − 93 = 7 pregnancies per 100 users.
Male condom under typical use: 100 − 87 = 13 pregnancies per 100 users.
Condom gap between perfect and typical use: 98 − 87 = 11 points.
Implant and IUD sit above 99% in both columns, so their gap is close to 0.
worked_example.answer: About 7 and 13 pregnancies per 100 users a year, so counsel from the typical-use column.

mistakes: Counselling from perfect-use figures. They describe laboratory conditions.
Promoting LARC through targets or insertion incentives, which recreates the problem Cairo ended.
Stopping at pregnancy prevention. A woman with an IUD may still need condoms and will not be told unless asked.
Requiring partner consent. It is not required, and demanding it is a rights violation.

recall.q: Which contraceptive method is the only one that protects against STIs?
recall.a: Condoms.

recall.q: What does LARC stand for, and what is its rights condition?
recall.a: Long-acting reversible contraception; removal on request must be guaranteed.

recall.q: What is the typical-use effectiveness of the pill and the male condom?
recall.a: About 93% and about 87%.

recall.q: Why does NFHS unmet need understate the gap?
recall.a: It covers only currently married women, leaving unmarried people out.

recall.q: What is the strongest predictor of continuation?
recall.a: Honest side-effect counselling.

sections.title: Pregnancy & Maternal Health
sections.big_idea: Most maternal deaths have cheap, known remedies, so the task is delivery and equity. **Check the postnatal link and disaggregate**, because averages hide where women die.
in_plain_words: Care runs as a continuum: pre-pregnancy, antenatal, childbirth and postnatal. Institutional delivery rose from about 39% in NFHS-3 to 79% and then 89% in NFHS-5, so childbirth is largely closed. The weak links sit either side of it. Antenatal care is defined by testing for pre-eclampsia, anaemia, syphilis and HIV, and a visit that only records weight does not count.

Haemorrhage, eclampsia, sepsis, obstructed labour and unsafe abortion each have a known remedy. MMR was 88 in 2021–23 (93 in 2019–21) against an SDG floor of 70, with Kerala at 30 and the highest-burden states between 141 and 153. Risk stays high in the first 24 to 48 hours and the first week, and nobody may be watching. Cut data by wealth, state, district, caste and tribe.

diagram.caption: the chain now breaks at both ends and holds in the middle

key_terms.meaning: Maternal deaths per 100,000 live births.
Antenatal care: monitoring, screening, supplements and birth planning.
The 2011 scheme removing every facility charge, caesarean included.
Home-based newborn care; visits for institutional births start on day three.
The Sample Registration System, India's authoritative source for MMR.

worked_example.title: Three gaps in numbers
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's figures for institutional delivery, MMR and the state spread.
steps: Institutional delivery rose from 39% to 89%: 89 − 39 = 50 percentage points.
Over fifteen years that is 50 ÷ 15 = 3.3 points a year.
MMR gap to the SDG 3.1 floor in 2021–23: 88 − 70 = 18 per 100,000 live births.
State spread: the highest-burden state at 153 against Kerala at 30 means 153 ÷ 30 = 5.1 times.
worked_example.answer: 50 points in fifteen years, 18 above the floor nationally, and about 5.1 times between the highest state and Kerala.

mistakes: Assuming 89% institutional delivery means safe delivery. Readiness, staffing, drugs and blood still decide.
Counting a visit as antenatal care when it only records weight and dispenses tablets.
Quoting the national MMR when the spread between states and districts directs resources.
Overlooking the postnatal window, where a woman discharged within hours is home before the first visit.

recall.q: What did institutional delivery reach in NFHS-5?
recall.a: About 89%.

recall.q: How many antenatal contacts does WHO recommend?
recall.a: At least eight.

recall.q: Name two direct causes of maternal death and their remedies.
recall.a: Haemorrhage with oxytocin and blood; eclampsia with magnesium sulphate.

recall.q: What is India's SDG 3.1 target?
recall.a: A national maternal mortality ratio below 70 per 100,000 by 2030.

recall.q: Why is the district the level where gaps become actionable?
recall.a: It often shows a wider spread than between states, and state averages are too coarse.

sections.title: Safe Abortion & the Law
sections.big_idea: Abortion is legal in India on specified grounds, and wrongful refusal comes mostly from misunderstanding. **The gap between legality and access is operational.**
in_plain_words: Restricting abortion leaves the number about the same and changes who performs them and how safely. The MTP Act, 1971 permits abortion by a registered practitioner on grounds including risk to health, substantial fetal abnormality, rape and contraceptive failure. The 2021 amendment extended the contraceptive-failure ground to any woman. Spousal or parental consent is not required for an adult woman.

The gestation bands are: up to 20 weeks one practitioner, 20 to 24 weeks two practitioners for specified categories, and beyond 24 weeks only fetal abnormality via a Medical Board or saving the woman's life. The PCPNDT Act bans sex determination and does not restrict legal abortion, and confusing the two is the commonest legal error. Good abortion care is a package that includes pain management and post-abortion contraception.

key_terms.meaning: The 1971 Act on when abortion may lawfully be performed, amended in 2021.
The 1994 Act banning sex determination; it does not restrict legal abortion.
The State body that considers cases beyond 24 weeks.
Care owed however the abortion happened, including contraception.
Abortion by an untrained provider, unsafe method or unsupervised self-medication.

worked_example.title: Which approval applies?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: three clients present at 18 weeks, 22 weeks, and 26 weeks with a substantial fetal abnormality.
steps: 18 weeks is up to 20 weeks, so the opinion of one registered medical practitioner is enough.
22 weeks falls in 20 to 24 weeks, so two practitioners, for categories specified in the rules.
26 weeks is beyond 24 weeks, where substantial fetal abnormality goes through a State Medical Board.
At every stage confidentiality is protected, and disclosure is an offence.
worked_example.answer: One practitioner, two practitioners, then a Medical Board.

mistakes: Asking an adult woman for spousal or parental consent. The law does not impose it.
Treating the PCPNDT Act as a limit on abortion. It restricts disclosure of fetal sex only.
Refusing unmarried women. The 2021 amendment extended the contraceptive-failure ground to any woman.
Offering abortion without pain management or post-abortion contraception, which leaves her to return in the same situation.

recall.q: Which year did the MTP Act pass, and which amendment widened access?
recall.a: 1971; the 2021 amendment.

recall.q: How many practitioners are needed at 20 to 24 weeks?
recall.a: Two, for categories specified in the rules.

recall.q: What is the main cause of wrongful refusal?
recall.a: Provider confusion between the MTP Act and the PCPNDT Act.

recall.q: What does restricting abortion do to the number of abortions?
recall.a: Leaves it about the same and makes them less safe.

recall.q: Name three parts of abortion care beyond the procedure.
recall.a: Information and counselling, pain management, post-abortion contraception, dignity and confidentiality.

sections.title: STIs & HIV
sections.big_idea: Most STIs are silent, so testing is the only way to know. **Stigma is a transmission mechanism**, and HIV is now a manageable condition.
in_plain_words: Bacterial and parasitic STIs are curable, and viral ones are manageable. Untreated chlamydia and gonorrhoea lead to infertility, syphilis in pregnancy to stillbirth, and HPV to cervical cancer. Prevention combines condoms at every act, testing, HPV vaccination before sexual debut and partner treatment. Partner treatment is the step most often skipped.

HIV spreads through unprotected sex, infected blood, shared injecting equipment and from mother to child, and never through food, hugging or mosquitoes. With lifelong ART the virus becomes undetectable and untransmittable (U=U). PrEP prevents infection, and PEP works within 72 hours of exposure. The HIV/AIDS Act, 2017 prohibits discrimination. Fear of judgement drives people away from testing and treatment.

key_terms.meaning: An infection passed mainly through sexual contact; many cause no symptoms.
Antiretroviral therapy: lifelong, free in India's public system.
Undetectable equals untransmittable: no sexual transmission on effective ART.
Medicine before possible exposure, and emergency medicine within 72 hours after.
Treatment in pregnancy to prevent HIV passing to the baby.

worked_example.title: The PEP clock
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a person is exposed to HIV at 9 pm on a Monday. The deck says PEP works within 72 hours, and the sooner the better.
steps: The window is 72 hours.
Three days after Monday 9 pm is Thursday 9 pm, so the window closes then.
Because sooner is better, the practical rule is to start as early as possible and not to wait for the deadline.
worked_example.answer: The window closes at Thursday 9 pm, and the target is to start at once.

mistakes: Diagnosing by symptoms. No symptoms is the norm, and syndromic management misses the silent cases.
Treating one partner only, which produces a cycle that looks like treatment failure.
Believing casual contact transmits HIV, which drives unlawful exclusion from schools and workplaces.
Screening for cervical lesions with no recall and treatment pathway, which finds women and loses them.

recall.q: Which STIs are curable?
recall.a: Bacterial and parasitic ones, such as chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis and trichomoniasis.

recall.q: What does U=U mean?
recall.a: When the virus is undetectable on ART, it is not sexually transmitted.

recall.q: Within what time must PEP start?
recall.a: Within 72 hours, and the sooner the better.

recall.q: Which law prohibits HIV-based discrimination?
recall.a: The HIV/AIDS Act, 2017.

recall.q: Why is HPV vaccination ideally given before sexual debut?
recall.a: It is most effective then, so the intervention sits in adolescent health.

sections.title: Sexuality Education (CSE)
sections.big_idea: CSE is age-appropriate, rights-based and wider than biology. **Rigorous reviews find it does not raise sexual activity** and does improve safety.
in_plain_words: CSE teaches knowledge, skills and values, plus where to get services. Consent, power, coercion and refusal are the safeguarding core, while anatomy and contraception are usually all that 'sex education' includes. Content is incremental: body autonomy and safe touch early, puberty at pre-teen, consent and relationships in early adolescence, contraception and services later.

UNESCO and WHO reviews find no earlier debut, no more partners and no more activity, with more contraceptive use among the active and better recognition of abuse. Abstinence-only programmes do not delay debut. Quality and dose matter. Answer myths with evidence and use life-skills framing. In India delivery is uneven because of state adoption, teacher training and local objection.

levels.label: Early primary
levels.sub: names, safe touch, who to tell

key_terms.meaning: Age-appropriate, scientifically accurate, rights-based teaching on bodies, relationships, consent and rights.
Content that builds with age instead of one curriculum for all.
Programmes that do not delay debut and link to less contraceptive use.
Naming CSE adolescent health or life skills, which meets less resistance.
UNESCO's guidance on what age-appropriate CSE looks like.

worked_example.title: Answer the objection
worked_example.setup: Four objections arrive at a parent meeting. Pair each with the deck's response.
steps: 'It encourages sex': repeatedly tested, and no such effect is found.
'Too much, too young': content is matched to developmental stage.
'Against our culture': consent, respect and safety are not foreign values.
'Silence keeps children safe': silence is what abusers rely on, so lead with this one.
worked_example.answer: Four short answers, with child safety as the lead.

mistakes: Teaching biology alone. The skills that let a young person recognise coercion are the part that changes outcomes.
Treating the first row of the age table as sex education. It is child protection.
Judging CSE by one assembly. A sustained, trained, age-appropriate curriculum delivers most of the effect.
Ignoring teacher confidence. Discomfort with the material is commonly the main obstacle.

recall.q: Does good CSE increase sexual activity?
recall.a: No. Reviews find no earlier debut, no more partners and no more activity.

recall.q: What do abstinence-only programmes do to debut?
recall.a: They do not delay it.

recall.q: Name two outcomes that rise with CSE.
recall.a: Knowledge, contraceptive and condom use among the active, or recognition of abuse.

recall.q: What is the status of CSE in India?
recall.a: Delivered through several programmes, with no uniform national curriculum.

recall.q: Which sources review the evidence?
recall.a: UNESCO and WHO.

sections.title: Gender, Consent & GBV
sections.big_idea: Consent is free, informed, specific, reversible and ongoing, and all five must hold at once. **Where refusing has a cost, agreement is not consent.**
in_plain_words: Silence, a previous yes, pressure or deception, incapacity and being under 18 all fail as consent. The freeze response explains why not fighting back is no evidence of consent. GBV drives unintended pregnancy, STIs, poor maternal outcomes and non-use of services, so a provider seeing SRHR clients is seeing survivors. NFHS-6 records 22.3% of ever-married women aged 18–49 with spousal violence, down from 29.2%.

A survivor-centred response puts safety first, protects confidentiality, leaves the choice to the survivor, avoids judgement and refers. POCSO covers everyone under 18 and makes reporting mandatory, which strains adolescent confidentiality. The legal age of marriage is 18 for women and 21 for men. LGBTQ+ inclusion means services that assume neither heterosexuality nor a gender.

diagram.caption: all five must be true at the moment

key_terms.meaning: Clear, freely given, informed, specific, reversible and ongoing agreement.
Harmful acts directed at a person because of gender, rooted in inequality and abuse of power.
The 2012 Act on sexual offences against anyone under 18, with mandatory reporting.
A common reaction to fear; it explains why no resistance is not consent.
Safety, confidentiality, choice, non-judgement and referral.

worked_example.title: Test sterilisation consent
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a woman is asked to accept sterilisation immediately after delivery, as a condition of receiving a benefit. Apply the practical tests.
steps: Freely given: could she have said no without cost? No, because the benefit depends on yes.
Informed: does she know what is proposed? Check, but the first test already fails.
Specific and reversible: consent must be to this act, and a change of mind must be respected.
Ongoing: ask whether it has been checked this time.
worked_example.answer: It fails the first test, so agreement is not consent.

mistakes: Reading silence or lack of resistance as consent. Freezing is a common response to fear.
Treating a past yes as covering later acts. Consent is specific and ongoing.
Promising a minor total confidentiality when POCSO imposes a mandatory duty to report.
Pressing a survivor for details you do not need. Repeated retelling is itself harmful.

recall.q: List the five features of real consent.
recall.a: Freely given, informed, specific, reversible, ongoing.

recall.q: Below what age can a person not consent to sexual activity in India?
recall.a: 18, under POCSO.

recall.q: Name the five parts of a survivor-centred response.
recall.a: Safety first, confidentiality, choice, non-judgement, referral.

recall.q: What is the legal minimum age of marriage?
recall.a: 18 for women and 21 for men.

recall.q: What does NFHS-6 show for spousal violence among ever-married women aged 18–49?
recall.a: 22.3%, down from 29.2% in NFHS-5.

sections.title: Adolescents & Access
sections.big_idea: Almost no adolescent barrier is legal. **Attitude, confidentiality and design decide access**, and a service can change all three.
in_plain_words: Adolescence runs roughly ages 10 to 19. Needs such as puberty information, contraception, STI testing, care after violence and safe abortion meet barriers: late information, reluctant providers, fear that parents will find out, and mandatory reporting. The MTP Act, contraception and STI services do not require marriage.

RKSK covers several priority areas, including SRH, and works through peer educators and adolescent-friendly clinics. Confidentiality needs time alone and limits stated before any disclosure. A youth-friendly service is accessible, acceptable, equitable, effective and confidential. Reach young people through peers, schools, phones and outreach, and note each channel's limit: out-of-school adolescents are reached by the costliest channel.

children.label: Operational
items: No privacy in the consultation space

children.label: Legal
items: No row in the deck's table

diagram.caption: each barrier is something a service can change

key_terms.meaning: Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram, India's national adolescent health programme.
Adolescent Friendly Health Clinic, run under RKSK.
A young person trusted by other young people; needs real training.
A whole way of working: accessible, acceptable, equitable, effective, confidential.
Abuse or serious risk of harm, stated up front.

worked_example.title: Pick the channel
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a district team must reach three groups of adolescents. Use the channel table.
steps: Girls still enrolled in school: schools reach those enrolled, though they miss the most vulnerable.
Out-of-school adolescents: community outreach, the slowest and most staff-intensive channel.
A girl whose phone access is mediated by her family: digital channels look equitable and are unequal for girls.
Add peer educators for those inside the peer network, which needs real training and support.
worked_example.answer: Schools, outreach and peer educators, with phones treated carefully.

mistakes: Treating the refusals as legal. The deck finds no legal barrier among them.
Stating the limits of confidentiality after a disclosure. The young person has already been misled.
Building a separate adolescent room and calling it youth-friendly while staff stay judgemental.
Assuming phone-based channels are equitable when a girl's phone is mediated by her family.

recall.q: Name three RKSK priority areas.
recall.a: Any three of sexual and reproductive health, nutrition, mental health, substance misuse, injuries and violence, non-communicable diseases.

recall.q: Is any barrier in the deck's table legal?
recall.a: No. Each is attitudinal or operational.

recall.q: When should the limits of confidentiality be stated?
recall.a: At the start, before any disclosure.

recall.q: What is the biggest factor in a youth-friendly service?
recall.a: Provider attitude.

recall.q: Which channel reaches out-of-school adolescents?
recall.a: Community outreach, which is the slowest and least funded.

sections.title: SRHR in South Asia & Practice
sections.big_idea: Coverage has moved faster than quality and equity. **Ask who is still being missed**, and verify a rule before you refuse anyone care.
in_plain_words: South Asia has gained on maternal mortality, contraception and institutional delivery, and lags on the spread between states and districts, the method mix, quality inside facilities and services for unmarried young people. Silence about sex, menstruation and abortion is itself a barrier. Work through trusted local voices and name the consequence, leaving the belief alone.

Gaps are widest for rural areas, unmarried adolescents, Dalit and Adivasi communities, LGBTQ+ people and persons with disabilities. Know the platforms: ASHA and ANM, RKSK, JSY and JSSK, NACO and One Stop Centres. Counselling is non-judgemental, confidential, complete and inclusive, and it supports the person's own decision. Most wrongful refusals come from a believed rule that does not exist.

diagram.caption: learn the pathway before the moment of disclosure

key_terms.meaning: Asking who is still being missed after asking how the average is doing.
Frontline workers who are the backbone of SRHR delivery.
The National AIDS Control Organisation, which leads India's HIV response.
A centre giving integrated support to survivors of violence.
A provider's objection, which carries a duty to refer onward.

worked_example.title: Check the rule
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: an unmarried 17-year-old asks a clinic for contraception. A colleague says a marriage certificate or spousal consent is required.
steps: Ask where the requirement comes from. If you cannot cite it, treat it as habit and not law.
The deck says contraception does not require marriage, and partner consent is not required for contraception.
State the limits of confidentiality at the start, and offer time alone.
Offer the full range of methods and ask about STI risk separately, then support her decision.
If abuse is disclosed, POCSO's mandatory reporting applies.
worked_example.answer: Serve her, because no law requires marriage, and keep the POCSO duty in view.

mistakes: Telling communities to leave the platforms and practices they use. Name the consequence and work with trusted local voices.
Reading averages as progress for everyone. Every gain was achieved while five groups moved least.
Starting to look up the referral centre at the moment of disclosure.
Omitting a method you personally disapprove of. That withholds care while feeling you gave it.

recall.q: What is the shared pattern across the region's gains?
recall.a: Coverage moved while quality and equity lagged.

recall.q: Name three groups most likely to be missed.
recall.a: Any three of unmarried adolescents, Dalit and Adivasi communities, LGBTQ+ people, persons with disabilities, rural populations.

recall.q: What are the five principles of respectful counselling?
recall.a: Non-judgemental, confidential, complete information, support the person's decision, inclusive.

recall.q: What does the deck say about unverified requirements?
recall.a: If you cannot cite where a requirement comes from, treat it as a habit and not a law.

recall.q: Which source gives district-level data?
recall.a: The NFHS district fact sheets.

notes.2: Treat the agenda as the route through the course. Sections 1 and 2 give the meaning and the rights framework, 3 to 7 the clinical core, 8 and 9 education and consent, and 10 and 11 access and practice. Read in order, and use it later to **find a topic fast**.
notes.4: The WHO definition has a clause people drop: the possibility of pleasurable and safe experiences, free of coercion. Use the table to see how each framing changes a service. Only the well-being framing lets a provider **ask about relationships, coercion and consent**, which is how harm gets detected.
notes.5: Check any service against all four letters. Programmes tend to deliver the R and the H and omit the S and the second R, which is maternal and child health under a wider name. Use the closing test: **does it serve an unmarried person who is not pregnant and does not want to be?**
notes.6: Match each life stage to its need, then read the last column for who is actually served. Services are built around the married woman of reproductive age. The gap is rarely legal: the care is **not commissioned, staffed or measured**. Use the table as an audit of your own area.
notes.7: Each exclusion works through a default assumption and no written rule. The intake form, the poster and the counselling script simply do not imagine these groups. Read the table as a list of assumptions to remove. For disability the error runs **both ways**: presumed asexual, yet at higher risk of sexual violence.
notes.8: SRHR links to health and survival and to equality and opportunity. Remember one contrast in the SDG table: 3.7 measures service access and 5.6 measures whether the person decides. **A country can score well on one and badly on the other**, and indicator 5.6.1 is the one that measures autonomy.
notes.9: Language is the first thing a patient assesses, and it costs nothing to change. Learn the swaps in the table: describe behaviour and skip labels of character, say 'partner' for 'husband', say 'negative' for 'clean'. An open question such as 'Do you have a partner?' produces **accurate history**.
notes.10: This is the map of what follows: rights, the clinical core, CSE, gender and consent, then the South Asian context. Examples are India-centric and sources are named, so use them to **verify a claim and go deeper**. Return here when you need to locate a topic.
notes.12: SRHR invents no new rights. It applies life, privacy, equality, freedom from ill-treatment and information to sexuality and reproduction, so claims are **legally enforceable**. The torture row matters: coerced sterilisation counts as ill-treatment, which changed the legal status of the target-driven era.
notes.13: Cairo 1994 moved the agenda from demographic targets to individual rights. Learn the four swaps in the table: rights for population control, voluntary choice for quotas, quality of care for number of acceptors, gender equality for fertility as a technical problem. **179 governments endorsed it**, so it carries weight in national policy.
notes.14: Compare the two eras by how success was measured: acceptors before Cairo, need met and quality of care after. India dropped method-specific targets in 1996, and Devika Biswas (2016) closed sterilisation camps and set consent standards. Watch for **incentives attached to volume**, where the old pressure returns.
notes.15: Bodily autonomy means yes, no and deciding for yourself. Coercion runs in both directions, so pressure to be sterilised and pressure to keep bearing children are the same violation. When a payment is large relative to household income, **consent becomes hard to tell from inducement**.
notes.16: The 2018 Guttmacher–Lancet definition made SRHR checkable. Before it, 'we provide SRHR' could not be tested, and now a package can be compared with a named list. Use the table's four demands as an audit, and the gaps turn into **specific commissioning decisions**.
notes.17: Memorise the seven elements and run your programme against them. The table flags what is most often missing, including CSE, full method choice, safe abortion and GBV care. Integration also detects harm: a woman who comes for contraception is **someone a trained provider can screen for violence**.
notes.18: AAAQ is a conjunction of available, accessible, acceptable and quality. A stocked, free clinic with a staff member who shames patients delivers nothing, because **acceptability gates the rest**. It comes from General Comment 14 on the right to health, so it is a legal standard as well as a checklist.
notes.20: A child who can name body parts can describe what happened and is more likely to be believed. Euphemism also removes the words needed to consent or refuse. Use the table to swap 'down there' for correct terms, because **you cannot decline what you have no words for**.
notes.21: Puberty timing varies widely, so there is no single right age. Use the table to reassure: starting at 9 is within the normal range, and nothing by 14 deserves a check-up and is no emergency. Often **the distress is the presenting problem**, and information is the treatment. Early puberty in girls also raises a safeguarding concern.
notes.22: Learn the four phases and remember which part is stable. The luteal phase lasts about 14 days, and the follicular phase is what varies. That makes 'day 14' **unreliable as a rule**. Irregular cycles are common in the first two years after menarche and near menopause, exactly when calendars get relied on.
notes.23: The fertile window is wider than a day: sperm survive several days, the egg lasts about a day, and ovulation moves between cycles. Counsel fertility awareness as a real option with honest numbers. Typical use is **well below perfect use**, and the gap is larger here than for most methods.
notes.24: MHH has four parts: clean materials, a private space with water and soap, safe disposal, and freedom from stigma. The infrastructure items are the ones a programme can fix directly. **Information before menarche** is the item most often mistimed, since sessions arrive after many girls have started.
notes.25: Every restriction in the table is cultural and has no health basis, and one of them kills: seclusion has caused deaths, which is why Nepal criminalised chhaupadi. Argue with the practical consequences. **Toilets with water and doors, affordable materials and pain relief** change more than confronting custom.
notes.26: Use the table to separate symptoms that deserve a check-up from ones people put up with. Endometriosis is the clearest case of 'normalised until diagnosed', with diagnosis delayed by years. Bleeding after sex is the one **never to normalise**. Normalising help-seeking is part of the job.
notes.28: Family planning works on the denominator: it cuts maternal death by reducing the number of pregnancies and makes no single one safer. The operative phrase is **informed, voluntary choice**. A method accepted under pressure, an incentive or without honest side-effect information is not a chosen method.
notes.29: Learn the six families and the column that matters most: condoms are the only method that protects against STIs. Counsel sterilisation as permanent, since reversal is expensive and unreliable. LARC removes user error, and works as a choice only if **removal on request is guaranteed**.
notes.30: Always counsel from the typical-use column, since perfect use describes laboratory conditions. Read the gap as the real-world difference between methods: implant and IUD barely move, the pill falls from over 99% to about 93%, the male condom from about 98% to about 87%. **The gap is largest where action is needed at each act.**
notes.31: The chart ranks methods by typical-use effectiveness, with rounded figures that vary slightly by source. LARC leads because it needs no daily or per-act action. The rights condition comes with it: **removal on request must be guaranteed**. Promote LARC on effectiveness, never through targets or insertion incentives.
notes.32: Condoms do two jobs: preventing pregnancy and preventing STIs including HIV. Read the table by column. A LARC alone gives excellent pregnancy prevention and no infection protection. **Ask both questions at every consultation**: what do you want to prevent, and with whom?
notes.33: Emergency contraception is a backup that works mainly by delaying or preventing ovulation. It does not end an established pregnancy, and it protects against no STIs. The abortion myth **leads to refusal at the pharmacy counter**, exactly when delay lowers effectiveness. It is available without prescription in India.
notes.34: Good counselling makes family planning rights-based. Use the five steps as a checklist: full range, honest side effects, a separate STI question, permission to switch or stop, and removal on request. Honest side-effect counselling is **the strongest predictor of continuation**.
notes.35: Unmet need is the share who want to avoid or delay pregnancy and use no method. The table shows total unmet need falling to 8.5% from 9.4%, while modern use fell to 52.7%. NFHS measures only married women, so **the unmarried sit outside the denominator** and the headline understates the gap.
notes.36: The chart shows the trend and is illustrative. Keep the NFHS-5 facts: about 57% modern use, about 67% any method, and a total fertility rate about 2.0, below replacement. With fertility already low, **choice is the only legitimate rationale** for family planning, and the task is method mix and quality.
notes.37: The skew is the finding: female sterilisation at about 38% against about 0.3% for male sterilisation, and more use than all other methods combined. That reflects programme history and provider incentives. Vasectomy is simpler, safer and cheaper. **A balanced method mix** marks a maturing programme.
notes.38: Men's involvement shapes whether women can use any method. The table pairs each barrier with what shifts it: accurate information from men who have had vasectomy, services that address men, timings that spare a day's pay, male providers and privacy. **Partner consent is not required by law**, and demanding it violates rights.
notes.40: Trace the four stages and ask where women fall out. Childbirth is largely closed at 89% institutional, while pre-pregnancy and postnatal care are weak. Ask of any district: of women who delivered in a facility, **how many had a postnatal contact within 48 hours?** The drop is the continuum failing.
notes.41: ANC is defined by what is tested. Each component in the table finds something the woman would never report: pre-eclampsia, anaemia, syphilis and HIV, fetal position. A visit that records weight and hands out tablets is **not antenatal care**. WHO recommends eight contacts, and NFHS-6 reports 65.2% with at least four.
notes.42: Read the scheme dates as a strategy. JSY (2005) got her to come, JSSK (2011) made it cost nothing, and transport and quality schemes made the arrival worth it. A skilled attendant protects only if the facility can manage an emergency, so **institutional delivery becomes a readiness problem**.
notes.43: The chart is illustrative, and the table gives the numbers: about 39% in NFHS-3, 79% in NFHS-4 and 89% in NFHS-5. That is fifty percentage points in fifteen years. Remember the tail: home births stay concentrated among **the poorest, Adivasi communities and remote blocks**.
notes.44: MMR is maternal deaths per 100,000 live births. The table lists five causes with cheap remedies: oxytocin, magnesium sulphate, antibiotics, a timely caesarean and safe abortion. This is **a delivery and equity problem**, since the remedies are old. Unsafe abortion vanishes when services are legal, available and free of stigma.
notes.45: The chart shows the SRS trend, and the table gives the anchors: 93 in 2019–21 and 88 in 2021–23, against an SDG 3.1 floor of 70. SRS samples, so small-state estimates are unstable. The national figure hides a spread: **Kerala at 30, the highest-burden states between 141 and 153**.
notes.46: The postnatal window is dangerous and thinly watched. In the table, the second row has nobody watching: a woman discharged within hours is home before HBNC visits start on day three. Add postpartum depression, which is common, treatable and **almost never screened for**.
notes.47: Averages hide where women die. Cut maternal data by wealth quintile, state, district, and caste and tribe. The district is where the gap becomes actionable, because state averages are too coarse to direct resources. The one-line rule is **disaggregate before you conclude**.
notes.49: Safe abortion is health care, and the table shows three situations. The middle row describes India: legal but hard to reach, so unsafe abortion persists at scale. Restriction leaves the **number of abortions about the same** and changes who performs them and how safely.
notes.50: Learn the four grounds, and learn what the law does not require: spousal or parental consent for an adult woman. The grounds are wider than most providers and clients believe, and wrongful refusal is driven by misunderstanding of the Act. It is **abortion on specified grounds** at every stage, and no request alone suffices.
notes.51: Remember the three gestation bands: up to 20 weeks needs one practitioner, 20 to 24 weeks two, and beyond 24 weeks only fetal abnormality via a Medical Board or saving life. The contraceptive-failure ground for any woman matters most in practice. The Act protects the provider, so **access depends on a willing one**.
notes.52: Abortion care is a package: information and counselling, a method suited to the gestation, pain management, post-abortion contraception, dignity and confidentiality. The table lists what goes missing. **Post-abortion contraception** has the clearest downstream effect, and pain relief is often omitted for reasons that are not clinical.
notes.53: Keep the two Acts apart. The MTP Act sets when abortion is lawful, and PCPNDT bans sex determination and restricts disclosure of fetal sex. A provider who thinks PCPNDT covers any abortion refuses lawful care. **Both can be respected at once**: never determine or disclose fetal sex, and provide abortion within the MTP Act.
notes.54: Restricting safe care makes abortions less safe without lowering their number. The table traces four routes to harm. The fourth is created by services: every week of refusal or searching moves a woman toward a **higher-risk procedure**. Post-abortion care is owed however the abortion happened.
notes.55: Read the barrier table as a fix-list. Four of the five need no change in law: non-judgemental care, plain-language guidance, district certification and written separation from PCPNDT. Legality and access differ because of **operations: training, guidance and provider attitude**. Medical abortion needs correct dosing information and a route to care.
notes.57: The key fact is that having no symptoms is the norm. That makes symptom-based diagnosis unreliable and testing the only way to know. Use the table to separate curable bacterial and parasitic infections from viral ones, which are manageable. Syndromic management **misses the silent cases** by definition.
notes.58: Four prevention tools, each with a timing in the table: condoms every act, regular testing if at risk, HPV vaccination ideally before sexual debut, and partner treatment at the same time as the index case. Partner treatment is the step most often skipped, producing **a cycle that looks like treatment failure**.
notes.59: Learn the transmission routes, then the list of what does not transmit HIV: food, utensils, toilets, hugging, mosquitoes, working alongside. The right-hand column is why stigma persists, because none of it has any basis. The HIV/AIDS Act, 2017 makes **exclusion unlawful** as well as unfounded.
notes.60: With treatment HIV becomes manageable, and undetectable means untransmittable (U=U). ART is lifelong and free in India's public system, so adherence is the whole intervention and cost is rarely the barrier. U=U is little known even among providers, so **telling the person is part of the care**.
notes.61: Know four tools: PMTCT, PrEP, PEP and condoms. The operational fact is the PEP window of 72 hours, which most people do not know, including after sexual assault. PMTCT works in the large majority of cases when started in time, which is why **HIV testing is routine in antenatal care**.
notes.62: Stigma is a transmission mechanism: each row turns a social response into an epidemiological outcome. Avoiding tests leads to late diagnosis, and silence to untreated partners. Language does measurable work, so prefer **'person living with HIV'** to 'AIDS patient' or 'victim', and 'acquired' to 'caught'.
notes.63: Use the first table as a quick reference, then read the second as consequences: untreated chlamydia and gonorrhoea lead to infertility, syphilis in pregnancy to stillbirth, HPV to cervical cancer. Each began as a mostly symptomless infection, which is **the argument for testing** before anyone complains.
notes.64: Cervical cancer is among the most preventable cancers and still a leading cause of cancer death among women in the region. The table lists four steps, each needing a delivery system. Heed the warning on screening: **without recall and treatment it finds women and then loses them**.
notes.66: CSE is wider than biology. The table shows its core: consent and refusal, gender and power, recognising coercion, and where to get services. Anatomy and contraception are usually all that 'sex education' includes. The skills part is **what changes outcomes**, and programmes narrowed to biology show weaker results.
notes.67: CSE builds knowledge, skills and values, plus access. Knowing about condoms does not tell a person how to negotiate using one, so effects appear where skills and access are taught with facts. The cheapest item to add is **telling young people that a service exists and that they may use it**.
notes.68: Content is matched to age: body autonomy and safe touch early, puberty and online safety around pre-teen, consent and relationships in early adolescence, contraception and services later. The first row is child protection, and objections target it most. 'Too much, too young' **misreads one curriculum for all ages**.
notes.69: This is the finding to be able to quote: good CSE brings no earlier debut, no more partners and no more activity. It is linked with more contraceptive use among the active and better recognition of abuse. UNESCO and WHO reviews looked for the feared effect repeatedly. Abstinence-only programmes **do not delay debut**.
notes.70: The pattern is stable across UNESCO and WHO reviews of many studies: knowledge up, debut later or unchanged, partners unchanged or fewer, contraceptive use up, abuse better recognised. Quality and dose decide size. A single assembly delivers little, while **a sustained, trained, age-appropriate curriculum** delivers most of it.
notes.71: The chart is a schematic of direction and shows no measured size. Take the last table into a public argument: no evidence that CSE causes earlier debut, and no evidence that abstinence-only delays it. The real alternative on offer is abstinence-only, so **compare CSE with that**.
notes.72: Prepare a one-line answer to each objection. For sceptical parents lead with 'silence keeps children safe': a child with no words for their body cannot report abuse. Framing as life skills, adolescent health or child safety meets **far less resistance** while teaching substantially the same material.
notes.73: India has delivery platforms and uneven implementation: the Adolescence Education Programme, School Health and Wellness Ambassadors and RKSK, with no uniform national CSE curriculum. The constraint is state adoption, teacher training and local objection. Teacher **discomfort** is commonly the main obstacle, so training should build confidence.
notes.75: Learn the five conditions: freely given, informed, specific, reversible and ongoing, and hold them all at once. Agreeing once at the start settles nothing. Under POCSO a person below 18 cannot consent to sexual activity, a **bright line** that applies whatever the other party's age or the young person's stated willingness.
notes.76: Use the practical-test column as a quick check. The first test, 'could they have said no without cost?', is the one power distorts. A woman agreeing to sterilisation just after delivery, or as a condition of a benefit, **fails the first test** like any other case.
notes.77: Silence, a previous yes, pressure, incapacity and being under 18 all fail as consent. The freeze response explains why 'she did not fight back' is no evidence of consent, a fact worth stating plainly to families and colleagues. Within marriage **the clinical and ethical standard is the same**.
notes.78: GBV is both a rights violation and an SRHR driver. Each row in the table turns a violence problem into an outcome such as unintended pregnancy or STIs, so the two cannot be split into separate programmes. NFHS-6 shows 22.3% of ever-married women aged 18–49 with spousal violence, so **assume survivors are in your clinic**.
notes.79: A survivor-centred response has five parts: safety first, confidentiality, the survivor's choice, non-judgement and referral. Learn the helpline numbers and referral pathway before a disclosure. Mind the boundary on choice: where the survivor is a child, **POCSO makes reporting mandatory**. Avoid pressing for details you do not need.
notes.80: POCSO covers all sexual offences against anyone under 18 and makes failing to report an offence. This strains adolescent confidentiality, because it can deter disclosure. **Know the duty and say so up front.** The Act also means consensual activity between adolescents falls within it, which is much debated.
notes.81: The legal minimum age is 18 for women and 21 for men, so state the current law and check for updates. The table links child marriage to early pregnancy, dropout, less power and violence. NFHS-6 shows 20.1% against 23.3% in NFHS-5. **Keeping girls in secondary school** has the strongest evidence.
notes.82: Know the legal position: same-sex relations decriminalised in 2018, NALSA affirming transgender rights in 2014, the 2019 Act in force and criticised, same-sex marriage unrecognised. Decriminalisation alone gives no access. Fix **small concrete things**: a third gender option, asking about partners, using the name and pronouns a person gives.
notes.84: Adolescent needs emerge just as barriers peak. The table lists five needs with their barriers, and almost none is legal. The MTP Act, contraception and STI services do not require marriage, so refusals come from **provider attitude and clinic practice**. South Asia's large adolescent population makes the gap large.
notes.85: RKSK is deliberately broad, and the table lists its six areas: SRH, nutrition, mental health, substance misuse, injuries and violence, and non-communicable diseases. The areas interact in the same adolescent, so splitting them loses the links. Where RKSK underperforms, the usual cause is **peer educators untrained or unpaid**.
notes.86: Sort each barrier into legal, attitudinal or operational. In the table not one row is legal, so every one is something a service can change. Try the walk-through: ask an adolescent to describe the visit from arrival to exit, and **privacy failures become visible**.
notes.87: Offer time alone and state the limits of confidentiality at the start, before any disclosure. A young person who learns mid-sentence that you must report has been misled and will not return. Parents need not be told routinely. A consultation held in front of a parent **yields the history the parent expects**.
notes.88: Youth-friendly is a way of working across the whole service, and a separate room is a small part. Use the five tests in the table: accessible, acceptable, equitable, effective and confidential. A judgemental adolescent clinic is not youth-friendly. **Provider attitude** is the biggest factor and the cheaper thing to fix.
notes.89: Four channels, each with a limit. Peer educators need real training, schools miss the most vulnerable, phone access is unequal for girls, and outreach is slowest. The second limit matters most: out-of-school adolescents are at highest risk, and **the channel that reaches them costs most and is funded least**.
notes.91: Every row shows coverage moving while quality and equity lag, which is the region's current transition and its harder half. Maternal mortality, contraception, institutional delivery and adolescent services each have a gain and a gap. Son preference sits behind several, and **health services alone cannot shift it**.
notes.92: Silence leaves the harm in place. The table ranks approaches: confronting the belief hardens resistance, trusted local voices work slower but last, and reframing as health and safety is usually accepted. Most successful practice **names the consequence and leaves the belief alone**, letting people with standing carry the message.
notes.93: Five groups are most often missed: unmarried adolescents, Dalit and Adivasi communities, LGBTQ+ people, persons with disabilities, and rural populations. Ask 'who is still being missed?' after 'how is the average doing?' **Disaggregate the data you already hold** by caste, marital status, disability and distance.
notes.94: This is your referral map: ASHA and ANM in the village, RKSK for young people, JSY and JSSK for delivery, NACO for HIV, One Stop Centres after violence. Learn the pathway before a disclosure. **Keep helpline numbers to hand**: childline, women's helpline and HIV.
notes.95: Five principles, each ruling something out. The quiet one is the third: a provider who omits a method they disapprove of has withheld care while feeling they gave it. Where conscientious objection applies, it carries **a duty to refer onward**.
notes.96: No pitfall here is committed by someone trying to do harm. Each comes from targets, an assumed rule, discomfort or habit, which is why supervision and training fix them. Check the second row in your own service. Use the closing test: **did the person leave better informed, respected and free to decide?**
notes.97: Run the five checks before each contact: accuracy, judgement, privacy, inclusion, and law and pathway. The last catches the largest category of harm in the course: believing a requirement exists (spousal consent, marriage certificate, minimum age). **If you cannot cite where a requirement comes from, treat it as habit.**
notes.98: Match each source to its use. The NFHS district fact sheets are the most immediately useful item: contraceptive use, method mix, anaemia, institutional delivery and marriage age for your own district, free to download. UNESCO's guidance is the document to hand to **anyone arguing that CSE is inappropriate**.
notes.99: Pair each takeaway with the failure it prevents. The last one gates the others, since information given with visible judgement does not get used. The habit to keep is to **ask about partners, marital status, gender and what the person wants**. It costs one sentence and changes what you are told.
